ACTIONS TRANSITIVE PIN CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Your workflow is pinned to a SHA. Is what it loads?

Pinning a reusable workflow or composite action to a commit SHA proves that reference cannot be silently repointed. It proves nothing about what the file at that commit itself calls — if it references a third-party action by a mutable tag, your SHA pin never sees it. Paste a workflow below and this checks the one hop underneath every pinned reference.

For the transitive step, this page fetches the exact public file each pinned reference points to, straight from raw.githubusercontent.com — no server of ours sees the request. See "Privacy" below before using it on a workflow you'd rather not do that for.

1. Paste a workflow file

Copy the contents of a file from .github/workflows/.

Paste a workflow file above and click Check.

Findings

Top-level referenceKindResult

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies:

node check.mjs                    # scan .github/workflows under the current directory
node check.mjs /path/to/repo      # scan a specific checkout
node check.mjs --format json      # machine-readable
node check.mjs --fail-on-risk     # exit 2 if a pinned reference loads an unpinned one
node check.mjs --no-network       # top-level classification only, no fetch (offline)

Get check.mjs, analyze.mjs, and classify.mjs from the repo — stdlib only (Node's built-in fetch), nothing to install.

Common questions

If my uses: line is pinned to a commit SHA, isn't that already safe?

It proves that exact reference cannot be silently repointed. It does not prove anything about what the reusable workflow or composite action at that commit itself does. If that file has its own uses: line pointing at a third-party action by a mutable tag, your workflow still runs whatever code that tag currently resolves to — your SHA pin never sees it, because it only pins the one hop you wrote.

Is this a real, current gap, or a theoretical one?

Current as of 2026. GitHub's own Actions security roadmap names this exact gap and describes a planned workflow lockfile that would pin every direct and transitive action dependency by commit SHA, the way a go.sum pins a Go module graph — which means it is not solved by SHA pinning alone today. Existing pinning checkers, including this portfolio's own pinned-actions-check, are explicit that they check only the uses: lines in the workflow file you scan, not what a pinned reusable workflow or composite action loads underneath it.

Does this tool fetch things from GitHub on my behalf?

Yes, for the transitive check only, and only the exact files your pasted workflow's pinned references point to. The CLI fetches over plain HTTPS from raw.githubusercontent.com, unauthenticated, no token, no login. The browser page does the same fetch directly from your browser to raw.githubusercontent.com — nothing passes through any server of ours. If a fetch fails or the file cannot be found, that reference is reported as unresolved, never as clean.

What if the nested reference is a JavaScript or Docker action, not a composite action?

Those have no action.yml with further uses: lines to check, so there is nothing underneath them for this tool to find either way. A fetch that comes back empty for that reason is reported as unresolved, the same as a genuine fetch failure — this tool cannot tell the two apart from outside, so it never claims one when it might be the other.

Does a clean result mean my CI is safe from supply-chain attacks?

No. This checks one specific, narrow thing: whether a reference you have already pinned to a commit SHA loads something else by a mutable tag one hop underneath it. It is not a security audit and makes no claim about your repository's overall security posture.

Privacy. The workflow YAML you paste is read in this browser and never uploaded anywhere. If the fetch option above is checked, this page makes a direct browser request to raw.githubusercontent.com for each pinned reference's own definition file — a public GitHub CDN, unauthenticated, no cookies attached and no token of yours involved — and reads nothing else. Uncheck it to skip that step entirely and see only the top-level classification. There are no accounts, tracking cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

More: what is a transitive GitHub Actions dependency? · this checker vs. manually checking nested references

This checks one hop underneath a reference you already pinned. Pinning it in the first place is the sibling check: Pinned Actions Check flags any third-party action in your own workflow file that is not pinned to a commit SHA at all, the more common and more urgent gap. A pinned, fully-resolved reference graph still leaves other risks in a workflow: Actions Injection Check flags pwn-request checkouts and script injection from untrusted ${{ github.event }} expressions, and Actions Permissions Check flags a workflow or job with no explicit permissions: grant.

Free and open source. If this saved you from a supply-chain gap a top-level pin doesn't cover, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-manually-checking-nested-references.h.text:
← Actions transitive pin check

This checker vs. manually checking nested references

Names no specific product or company — this compares the free tool against the generic method every maintainer already has: clicking through to each pinned reusable workflow or composite action on GitHub and reading its own uses: lines by eye.

QuestionChecking by handThis tool
Reading one pinned reference's own fileOpen the commit on GitHub, find action.yml or the workflow file, read its uses: linesFetches the same public file from raw.githubusercontent.com and classifies each reference automatically
A workflow with a dozen pinned stepsA dozen separate page loads and reads, one at a timeOne paste, one pass over every pinned reference in the file
Re-checking after a dependency bumpEasy to skip because it is slow, which is exactly when a reference most needs re-checkingCosts nothing extra to run again; the CLI can also run unattended in CI with --fail-on-risk
Telling "unpinned underneath" from "couldn't tell"A failed or slow page load looks the same as one you didn't get to yetA fetch that fails is reported as unresolved, never folded into a clean result
Judgment about whether your CI is safe overallA careful human reading brings context this tool has none ofChecks one narrow thing and says so — not a security audit

Neither method tells you whether a mutable tag it finds is itself trustworthy — both only establish whether a reference is pinned to a fixed commit or not.

Common questions

Can't I just click through to the pinned commit and read its uses: lines myself?

For one reference, yes — open the reusable workflow or composite action at the pinned commit on GitHub, read its action.yml or workflow file, and see whether its own uses: lines are pinned to a SHA or a mutable tag. This tool does exactly that fetch and that read, for every pinned reference in the workflow you paste, in one pass, and reports which ones load something unpinned underneath — rather than you repeating the click-and-read for each line by hand.

What does checking by hand actually miss?

Not correctness — a careful read of one reference by hand is as accurate as the tool's read of that same reference. What it misses is coverage: a workflow with a dozen pinned steps means a dozen separate page loads and reads, and a repository with many workflow files multiplies that by every file, every time a dependency is bumped. The check that gets skipped because it takes ten minutes is the check that misses the one reference that changed.

what-is-a-transitive-github-actions-depe.text:
← Actions Transitive Pin Check

What is a transitive GitHub Actions dependency?

Every uses: line in your own workflow file is a direct dependency — the thing you chose and, ideally, pinned yourself. A reusable workflow or a composite action is just another file with its own steps, and if one of those steps has its own uses: line, that is a transitive dependency: something your workflow depends on that you did not write, did not review, and cannot see by reading your own repository. Pinning your direct reference to a commit SHA fixes what that one line points to. It says nothing about what the file at that commit itself loads.

Where it hides

# your workflow — this line is pinned, and it is genuinely fixed
- uses: octo-org/shared-workflows/.github/workflows/build.yml@2c4d34e6cff37bafe66eba7a6c1c8a5c9d9c1a6e

# the file AT that commit — a step nobody reviewing your diff ever sees
- uses: some-third-party/build-helper@v3

Your SHA pin proves build.yml at that exact commit cannot be silently repointed to a different commit. It does not touch the second line, because that line lives in a file you neither wrote nor pinned. If some-third-party/build-helper's v3 tag is ever repointed — by its maintainer, or by whoever compromises that maintainer's account — every workflow that trusts your pinned reusable workflow inherits whatever code v3 now resolves to, on the next run, with no change to your own repository at all.

Why this is easy to miss

A top-level SHA pin is the well-known fix for the well-known problem: a mutable tag on a reference you wrote yourself. Reviewing that takes one look at your own workflow files. The transitive case takes fetching and reading a file that lives in someone else's repository, at a specific commit, before you can even tell whether there is anything to check — which is why most pinning checkers, this portfolio's own Pinned Actions Check included, are explicit that they classify only the uses: lines in the file you scan, and say nothing about what a pinned reusable workflow or composite action loads underneath it.

Check your own workflow

Paste a workflow into Actions Transitive Pin Check to fetch every pinned reference's own definition from raw.githubusercontent.com and flag one that loads something unpinned underneath, or run the CLI in your own repository:

node check.mjs --fail-on-risk

That exits nonzero if any pinned reference loads an unpinned one underneath it — wire it into your own CI to block a newly-introduced gap before it merges.

No warranty. This page and the tool it describes are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. This is not a security audit or a compliance attestation, and a clean scan does not mean a workflow is safe from supply-chain risk — only that this one specific gap was not found.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. Free, experimental, may move or go offline without notice.

The workflow YAML you paste in the linked tool is read in your browser and never uploaded; the transitive check makes a direct browser request to raw.githubusercontent.com for each pinned reference's own file, unauthenticated, and reads nothing else.
